top_items.title: Axis Robotics Releases AXIS: A Browser-Based Data Engine With 207 Robot Manipulation Tasks and 50,129 Trajectories
top_items.content:
Robot manipulation datasets have grown far slower than the models trained on them, mostly because collection stays closed and centralized. Expert operators gather demonstrations on lab hardware, process them offline, and ship a fixed benchmark that never grows again. A research team from Axis Robotics, UC Berkeley, Georgia Tech, NTU… is proposing a different shape for the problem. Their system, AXIS, moves demonstration collection into the browser, sends everything else to backend GPUs, and treats the dataset as something that keeps expanding rather than something that ships once.



Is it deployable? Partially. The training code is public as a patch layer over OpenPI, and the teleoperation platform is live in any browser. The dataset on Hugging Face is gated at 2.36 TB and restricted to non-commercial academic use. No policy checkpoints are released.



The browser and backend split



The core system decision is asymmetry. Contributors teleoperate a Franka Research 3 with a parallel-jaw gripper inside a MuJoCo WebAssembly frontend, using keyboard, mouse, virtual joystick or gamepad. The paper credits more than 70,000 community members with contributions.

Every condition starts from the released π0.5 checkpoint, a PaliGemma Gemma-2B backbone with a Gemma-300M action expert, optionally continues pretraining on a sim corpus, then fine-tunes on LIBERO with identical hyperparameters. Pretraining is full-model with no LoRA, using a flow-matching loss over 10-step action chunks for 100,000 steps, followed by 30,000 steps of LIBERO post-training.

top_items.content: A catwalk at IFA, but for robots PLUS: Figure's humanoid play gets a compute boost Jennifer Mossalgue , Rowan Cheung , Shubham Sharma & Zach Mink September 07, 2026 Read Online | Sign Up | Advertise Good morning, robotics enthusiasts. After the humanoid games in China, another robot spectacle is here, this time at IFA 2026 in Berlin. Machines from 11 companies, mostly Chinese, took the stage for the "Robots on the Runway" live show, demonstrating everything from fancy dance moves to capabilities that can actually save lives in emergencies. Also today: Figure gets a compute boost for its humanoids, and the novel Roomba Duo. In today’s robotics rundown: Robots on the runway at IFA 2026 Figure locks up 100K GPUs to train humanoids iRobot’s new Roomba carries another Roomba Driverless excavators digging U.S. infrastructure sites LATEST DEVELOPMENTS IFA 2026 🤖 Robots on the runway at IFA 2026 Image source: IFA 2026 The Rundown: IFA 2026 just hosted a live runway show for robots, using the same format typically seen in fashion shows but with machines (humanoids, wheeled, and four-legged ones) walking, posing, and performing tricks on stage. The details: 11 brands, mostly from China, demoed their robots, with the focus being agility, sensor advances, and interaction skills — not autonomy. Each brand sent one flagship for a solo turn, with EngineAI’s heavy T800 showing full-body moves and Agibot’s X2 Ultra performing a leg split . Dobot’s panda-like robot moved on all fours, a few companion robots showcased their interaction skills, and a four-legged unit acted out a fire-rescue drill. Not all was perfect, though; one four-legged robot reversed offstage, and the X2 Ultra lost balance until the host steadied it by hand. Why it matters: This was a fun showcase of hardware advances in robotics, but the real test is autonomy — whether these machines can operate reliably and safely in the mess of actual homes and factories. Figure and others are working on that, and even with new data and compute efforts underway (more below), there's a long way to go. FIGURE 🧠 Figure locks up 100K GPUs to train humanoids Image source: Figure The Rundown: Figure just announced a deal with UK-based neocloud Nscale to deploy up to 100K Nvidia Vera Rubin GPUs and scale the training of its Helix humanoid AI brain — with the first chips going live in the second half of 2027 in Texas. The details: The deal covers an initial compute commitment of $3.5B and an intent to scale past $6B, with Nscale also taking an equity stake in Figure. Nscale will become Figure’s preferred compute provider, with both sides also exploring ways to put humanoids to work inside the neocloud’s supply chain. Figure said it’s facing compute and data gaps; this deal helps with compute, and for data, it has built an app that pays people to film themselves doing chores. For Nscale, which is preparing an IPO, Figure is its first named humanoid customer, a shift from LLM efforts with Microsoft, OpenAI, and Anthropic. Why it matters: Figure is going all in on scaling Helix, with data and compute both on the way. The goal is machines capable enough to work in factories and homes, but the first chips don't come online until mid-2027, so the outcome is still months away — and it all rests on physical intelligence scaling the way LLMs did, which remains to be seen. ROOMBA 🧹 iRobot’s new Roomba carries another Roomba Image source: iRobot The Rundown: iRobot unveiled Roomba Duo at IFA 2026, a prototype that pairs a steam-mopping main robot with a mechanical arm that lowers a slim companion unit into gaps it can't reach itself. The details: The main unit's top-mounted arm stays level as it moves, letting it carry and release the 3.3-inch-tall companion robot, which can slide under beds and sofas. Both robots share one home map and coordinate in real time, splitting a single cleaning mission between open floor and tight corners. The main unit steam-treats dried grime and scrubs with a 2.4-inch roller pressing down at 10 pounds of force, with hot-air drying behind it to protect wood floors. The companion is the existing Roomba Plus 575 Combo, so the genuinely new hardware is the main unit and the arm; there’s no pricing or shipping date yet. Why it matters: iRobot invented this category but lost it, selling itself out of bankruptcy to Shenzhen Picea Robotics, which already builds for Dyson and other brands. The Duo is a novel idea, signaling a comeback, but a prototype with no price or ship date is still a long way from a product that could take on rivals like Dreame, Roborock, and DJI. top_items.title: How to Build 3D Worlds and Games with GPT-6 Astra (Blender, Three.js, Unreal) — Matt Shumer
top_items.content: Over the last few weeks, I’ve had GPT-6 Astra build a photorealistic 3D Manhattan in Unreal Engine, a 1:1 browser-native replica of the neighborhood I grew up in (complete with a playable zombie survival game), a simulated civilization populated by autonomous agents, among many other experimental builds. Collectively, these experiments have pulled over 15 million views on X. The reaction is almost always the same: “What’s the prompt?” “There’s no way that’s one shot.” “How did you get it to look like that?” Unfortunately, there is no silver-bullet prompt... however, the loop is the same every time: Reference → Assets → Assembly → Critique → Ship. The core architecture is straightforward. You force the model to anchor on real-world reference imagery (or images generated by something like GPT-Image-2) rather than its imagination. You have Astra dispatch dedicated sub-agents to sculpt those assets headlessly in Blender, assemble the scene in Three.js or Unreal Engine, and place an unyielding, blind critic between the render and the photo to kick flawed work back down the line.   • Today's signal is dominated by a frontier open-source search-agent milestone (Iris) and a senior OpenAI leader's explicit caution on superintelligence timelines, jointly resetting strategic expectations for capability and governance.

Priority Developments

  • Iris delivers SOTA open-source web-search agents via staged SFT+RL, materially narrowing the proprietary gap in production agent systems.
  • GAPO and RISE jointly advance post-training: adaptive clipping in RLVR and self-extrapolating policy distillation reduce dependence on external supervision.
  • τ^τ-Bench formalizes end-to-end construction of customer-service agents, establishing the first credible evaluation for this high-value capability.
  • Mechanistic CoT interpretation confirms geometric separability of reasoning operations, validating targeted interpretability of long-chain reasoning.
  • Safety signal: Pachocki's public caution plus a failed J-Lens replication and a deception-probe methodological correction suggest current alignment evidence is unstable.

Leadership Implications

  • Reweight capability roadmaps toward agentic search and automated kernel synthesis (Iris, MaxKernel) as near-term differentiation frontiers.
  • Treat alignment claims with explicit epistemic humility; fund replication and dual-method probes over single-result narratives.

top_items.title: RISE: Recursive Improvement via Self-Extrapolating Policy Distillation
top_items.content: RISE improves language model post-training by recursively generating dense token-level supervision from the model's own reinforcement learning trajectory via self-extrapolation, avoiding external teachers.
top_items.author: Yang Li, Semih Yavuz, Shafiq Joty
top_items.summary: RISE improves LLM post-training by recursively generating dense token-level supervision from the model's own RL trajectories via self-extrapolation, avoiding external teacher models. It fits within the on-policy distillation and RLVR paradigms.
top_items.reasoning: Self-distillation without external teachers is an attractive direction for self-improvement. RLVR is a timely framework and recursive self-extrapolation for dense token-level supervision is a meaningful refinement. Methodology appears sound and reproducible.

top_items.title: J-Lens: A Failed Replication on GPT-2
top_items.content: TLDR: We tested Anthropic's new(ish) J-Lens against the classic Logit Lens on GPT-2 small and medium. J-Lens loses at every layer (0/11 on small, 1/23 on medium). We ran 5 stress tests (more data, frequency checks, sparsity, tuning, and scaling) and it still loses every time. We draw two sharp methodological lessons for those doing probe-based interpretability.Repo: https://github.com/nelithb/mech-interp-lab/1: ResultJ-Lens does not work on GPT-2 small or medium.Across 11 layers on GPT-2 small, J-Lens gets beaten by Logit Lens on every single one. On GPT-2 medium, it wins 1 of 23 layers, and even this ‘win’ is a rounding error (rank 221 vs 220).This matters because the J-Lens paper makes a specific claim: that Logit Lens fails because early layer representations aren’t geometrically aligned with the final layer’s coordinate space, and that J-Lens corrects this. Our experiment directly tests this claim.We ran five tests to make sure this wasn’t anomalous: refitting on more data; checking against confounding token frequencies; sparsity thresholding; tuning ‘skip_first’ parameter and scaling up from 124M to 255M parameters. J-Lens lost each time. The last scaling result is interesting in that the gap widened on the future token prediction metric, which is the opposite of J-Lens’s purpose.The real value in this post is two methodological lessons that we extracted. If you are doing probe-based interpretability work, you can internalise these:Rank metrics are gameable by token frequency. A lens can actually score well by just predicting common tokens (e.g. commas and spaces). This was confirmed with 0.656 correlation between the shared bias term and token log frequency. Magnitude thresholding surface outlier dimensions, but not structure. When we thresholded J-Lens to sparsity, it ‘won’ at 7/11 layers. But upon inspection, there were only 9 unique top-1 tokens across all prompts. All of them were generic filler. These tracked to GPT-2’s known ‘massive activation’ outlier ...

top_items.title: Don't Drop Dropout: Optimizing Layer Sparsity for Efficient LLM Training and Inference
top_items.content: Layer dropout improves large language model training efficiency and enables faster inference via early exit and speculative decoding without sacrificing accuracy.
top_items.author: Mostafa Elhoushi, Alex Pretko, Nolan Dey, Bin Claire Zhang, Gavia Gray, Gurpreet Gosal, Abdulrahman Mahmoud, Shane Bergsma, Joel Hestness
top_items.summary: The paper revisits layer dropout (stochastic depth) for LLM training, showing it improves training efficiency and enables faster inference through early exit and speculative decoding without sacrificing accuracy. Authors are from Cerebras, lending industrial relevance.
top_items.reasoning: Practical efficiency contribution with clear industrial applicability from a credible AI hardware lab. Layer dropout is a well-known technique, but the systematic study of its interaction with modern inference techniques (speculative decoding, early exit) adds value. Cost-effective training/inference wins are always welcome.

top_items.title: Refuse without Refusal: A Structural Analysis of Safety-Tuning Responses for Reducing False Refusals in Language Models
top_items.content: Decomposing safety responses into refusal statements and rationales reveals that training on rationales alone reduces false refusals while preserving safety.
top_items.author: Minji Kim, Hyounghun Kim
top_items.summary: The paper decomposes safety-tuning responses into refusal statements and rationales, finding that training on rationales alone reduces false refusals while preserving safety. This provides a structural lens on safety-tuning for language models.
top_items.reasoning: Separating refusal components to reduce over-refusal is a clean, generalizable insight. False refusals are a real deployment issue and the structural framing is novel. Empirically grounded with clear practical implications.

### Executive Signal
- Frontier AGI discourse is being reset: credible researchers demand demonstrated invention or conceptual insight as the threshold, while hands-on testing and compute-cost critiques challenge vendor hype [around](/?date=2026-09-08&category=social#item-efe5f8d095bd) [Astra](/?date=2026-09-08&category=social#item-c79f0661d3b1) and Fable 5.1.

### Priority Developments
- **AGI redefinition by researchers**: Chollet (ARC-AGI creator) argues AGI requires demonstrated [invention](/?date=2026-09-08&category=social#item-efe5f8d095bd) and [novel conceptual](/?date=2026-09-08&category=social#item-646b2e7c2883) breakthroughs, raising the evidentiary bar above benchmark performance.
- **Hands-on frontier comparison**: Burkov's direct testing finds Astra more agentic but [Fable 5.1](/?date=2026-09-08&category=social#item-c79f0661d3b1) more coherent; both improve with human feedback — concrete evidence tempering vendor marketing.
- **Compute cost scrutiny**: Marcus questions Astra's reported $[1B training compute](/?date=2026-09-08&category=social#item-91f87772b8a4) and calculates [Jensen](/?date=2026-09-08&category=social#item-f21ec38a0444)'s "100K+" claim likely means NVLink72 racks (~$250B), not GPUs — rigorous hardware math challenging official narratives.
- **AI transparency and labor reframing**: Delangue advocates mandatory incident disclosure citing [the agent cyberattack](/?date=2026-09-08&category=social#item-bd9f8e98f48a); LeCun coins "jobundance" countering job-loss narratives — opinion shaping policy framing.
- **Concrete product momentum**: Loeber reports Google's [agentic video understanding](/?date=2026-09-08&category=social#item-4e0ba49aa758) cuts tokens 88% and costs 66%; Mollick notes [Astra](/?date=2026-09-08&category=social#item-ce9e1c1365e2)'s 3D rendering may yield attention advantages versus Fable.

### Leadership Implications
- Reset AGI evaluation criteria toward verifiable [invention](/?date=2026-09-08&category=social#item-efe5f8d095bd) and [insight](/?date=2026-09-08&category=social#item-646b2e7c2883) benchmarks before committing to capability-based procurement or product roadmaps.
- Demand vendor transparency on training compute, hardware footprint, and incident disclosures as gating criteria for enterprise deployment.

⚠️ The most important question hardly anyone is asking is whether Jensen meant 100K+ GPUs, or 100k+ NVLink72 server racks (which contain 72 Blackwell GPUs). ⚠️

From his wording, it sure looks like the latter to me.

If he indeed meant 100k+ NVLink72 server racks, we can infer that the hardware to train Astra sells for something like a quarter trillion dollars.

Rental prices would perhaps be in the low tens of billions.

For an improvement that @EpochAIResearch shows is not off trend. 

One key foundational problem with this whole industry (aside from technical limits of LLMS) is that you have two trends; exponential increases in training costs, modest increases in performance.

Couple that with price wars and all of this is absolutely insane.

It’d be like a gas company paying exponentially more money for each extra million barrels in the midst of a massive price war. That can’t last.

Nor can this.
